title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to teach K-12 students, specifically secondary students, to use generative AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning. The authors focus on "prompting literacy"—students’ ability to understand when AI can support learning, how to form effective prompts, and how to interact with AI in ways that support rather than replace learning. The study also examines whether an AI-based auto-grader can reliably assess student-written prompts and whether the accompanying assessments are suitable for measuring prompting literacy.

The intervention was a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based practice in which students wrote prompts for hypothetical learning situations in biology, geography, and math. Students interacted with an AI chatbot, then received AI-generated rubric-based feedback on their prompts. The module emphasized learning-by-doing and immediate elaborated feedback. Across two classroom deployment iterations, the authors evaluated the quality of the AI auto-grader, student performance on prompt-writing dimensions, confidence in using AI for learning, student perceptions of the experience, and the quality of assessment items. Study 1 used pre/post surveys, multiple-choice assessments, human-graded prompt artifacts, and thematic analysis of open-ended reflections; Study 2 revised the assessment to include true/false and open-ended items and analyzed item quality.

The population consisted of students in 11 authentic secondary education classrooms, with Study 1 explicitly reporting 111 valid student participants in six secondary classrooms in East Asia. Teachers were present to facilitate implementation in class. The setting was a classroom-based deployment of a web platform, with no control group. The paper does not report a multi-week duration; the intervention appears to have been delivered as an in-class practice activity with immediate post-activity measures.

The main conclusions are that the AI auto-grader achieved generally strong agreement with human grading, with average accuracy around 0.92, though some rubric dimensions were weaker than others. Students improved in including background/context in prompts and reported higher confidence in using AI for learning after the activity, while conceptual test scores showed no significant gain due to ceiling effects in the original assessment. Qualitative responses suggested students perceived the module as useful and engaging, especially the interactive AI practice and feedback. The second study showed that revised true/false and open-ended assessment items had better difficulty and discrimination characteristics than the original multiple-choice items. Overall, the paper presents promising early evidence for a scalable prompting-literacy module, while emphasizing the need for broader studies, stronger assessment design, and further refinement of the auto-grader and instructional materials.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom deployment study in authentic secondary settings with pre/post measures, human-validation of AI grading, and qualitative analysis, but it lacks a control group or random assignment and is primarily exploratory/design-based. The evidence is therefore direct K-12 but methodologically limited relative to causal standards.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings show positive but modest and uneven effects: confidence improved and one prompting dimension improved, while broader test gains were not significant and no literacy achievement outcomes were measured. Impact is therefore promising but unclear for general educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Web-based prompting literacy module in which secondary students interact with an LLM chatbot across biology, geography, and math learning scenarios to practice responsible AI use for learning.

AI auto-grader evaluates student-written prompts against a rubric and provides immediate elaborated feedback on dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, background/context, elaboration, and avoiding direct-answer seeking.
Scenario-based instructional platform delivering practice items, feedback, and assessments to teach prompting literacy in classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 111 secondary students in Study 1, students improved on one targeted prompting component—embedding background/context in prompts—over repeated practice, with McNemar test showing higher success on Q3 than Q1 (p=.039). However, there were no significant gains on relevance (p>.90), conciseness (p=.286), or purpose (p=.617), and no pre/post gain on the 6-item conceptual test among the 98 students completing both assessments (p=.377), indicating selective rather than broad prompting-literacy improvement.
finding.measure: Human-scored prompt quality by rubric dimensions across practice tasks; 6-item pre/post prompting-literacy assessment
finding.study_size: n=111 for classroom deployment; n=98 for matched pre/post test

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after the module, with self-reported confidence rising by 10.4% on average and a statistically significant Wilcoxon test (p<.001). Qualitative responses also indicated high interest in interacting with AI and favorable perceptions of the learning design, though some students reported challenges related to typing, login issues, and scenario relevance.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-reported confidence item and open-ended perception survey responses
finding.study_size: n=111 for confidence analysis; n=131 open-ended responses reported

finding.finding_summary: The AI auto-grader showed satisfactory agreement with human grading, achieving average pass/fail accuracy of 0.92 across rubric dimensions and overall explanation accuracy of 0.95. Accuracy was strongest for relevance (0.98), background (0.96), and elaboration (0.90), but weaker for purpose (0.85) and no-direct-answer judgments (0.88), suggesting the system can support scalable feedback with some reliability limitations.
finding.measure: Accuracy of AI auto-grading versus human rubric scoring; explanation accuracy

finding.finding_summary: Assessment revision in Study 2 improved item quality relative to the original multiple-choice version: 60% of open-ended items and 30% of true/false items fell into desired difficulty/discrimination ranges, whereas none of the original MCQs did. However, internal reliability remained only moderate and slightly lower for the iterated version (Cronbach's alpha 0.58 vs 0.68), so efficiency for robust measurement remains promising but not yet established.
finding.measure: Assessment item difficulty, discrimination, and Cronbach's alpha reliability
